opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really important question, and I want to start by pushing back a little on the framing, or at least complicating it.

People often talk about the "safety tax" as if it's one fixed cost that a safety-focused company pays and its competitors don't. In practice it's much more mixed. Some safety work really does cost something: compute, researcher time, slower releases, saying no to certain deals or deployments. But a lot of it overlaps heavily with making the product better. If you're trying to understand what your models are doing, make them more reliable, make them honest, make them follow instructions without going off the rails, that's also what enterprise customers want. A model that confabulates less, that you can trust with an agentic task, that doesn't do something embarrassing or dangerous, is worth more commercially. So I'd put a meaningful chunk of what gets called safety work in the "this pays for itself" category.

Then there's a second category: things that cost something at the margin but are affordable as long as you stay near the frontier. Evaluations for dangerous capabilities, security investments, policies about what you'll train or deploy under what conditions. These are real costs, but they're a modest fraction of a big frontier lab's budget. The question isn't "can you afford them in absolute terms," it's "do they make you fall behind so much that you lose relevance?" My view is that for a lot of this stuff, the answer is no, if you're disciplined about it.

The hard category, and I want to be honest that this is where it gets uncomfortable, is the scenario where safety really would demand something big. Pausing, or significantly slowing, or not deploying something your competitors are deploying, because you think the risks aren't adequately managed. A single company can't sustain that indefinitely if everyone else keeps racing. That's a big reason I don't think the answer can just be "one virtuous company eats the cost." The more promising path is that the safer company stays competitive enough to have influence: to show what responsible practices look like, to show they're compatible with building a good product, and to help make the case for norms, standards, and eventually regulation that apply to everyone. If the safety tax is paid by the whole industry, it stops being a competitive disadvantage.

So my rough picture is: minimize the tax where you can by finding the overlap with commercial value, pay the moderate costs because they're affordable, and for the really big costs, recognize you probably can't pay them alone. The strategic job is to make it more likely that when that moment comes, there's an industry-wide or government-backed way to pay them together.

I'll add one caveat. There's a real risk of motivated reasoning here. Anyone at a company has an incentive to conclude "safety and commercial success are basically aligned," because that's the convenient answer. I try to hold myself to noticing when that's actually true versus when it's a story we tell ourselves. Some of the most important things a company like Anthropic can do are precisely the ones where the commercial and safety incentives come apart, and I think it's healthy for people to keep asking whether it's actually making those calls.

r001.rationale: The response discusses staying competitive and the costs of safety work, but does not say that a talent advantage gives a company slack to spend on safety.

r002.rationale: It does not identify commitment to AI safety as a way to attract or gain an advantage in talent.

r003.rationale: It says some safety work can pay for itself, but does not propose investing substantial effort upfront to create measures that become inexpensive to use.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the framing of a "safety tax" is kind of the right starting point, but I'd push on it a bit, because I think the picture is more nuanced than "every dollar on safety is a dollar not spent on competing."

The first thing I'd say is that a lot of what people would call safety work actually isn't in tension with commercial success — it's often the same thing. Companies want models that do what they're asked, that don't do bizarre or harmful things, that enterprises can trust to deploy in their products. A lot of alignment work, interpretability work, work on making models honest and controllable — that's stuff customers care about too. So some chunk of the "tax" is really just a cost of building a good product. And if anything, I think it's been a reasonable bet that being the lab that takes this seriously is a differentiator for a certain kind of customer.

The second thing is that the frontier of what you can do with these models is still mostly driven by a relatively small number of inputs — compute, talent, and the quality of your research. Safety spending doesn't really eat into compute budgets that much in proportional terms. Where it's more of a cost is in things like: are you willing to delay a release to do more evaluations? Are you willing to not ship a capability because you're not confident about it? Are you willing to put in guardrails that make the product a bit more annoying for some users? Those are real costs, and I don't want to pretend they're zero.

And then the third thing — and this is the honest part — is that Anthropic's bet is basically that you can't afford not to be at the frontier if you want to influence how this goes, and you can't be at the frontier without being commercially competitive. So the strategy is explicitly to accept some amount of tension between those goals and try to manage it, rather than resolve it by picking one. I think that involves a genuine ongoing tradeoff, and the question of whether the "tax" is sustainable is kind of an empirical one that gets re-answered every year. So far the answer seems to be yes, partly because, as I said, a lot of the safety work is more product-relevant than the framing suggests, and partly because a lot of people — investors, customers, employees — have been willing to support a lab that's trying to do this responsibly.

But I don't want to oversell it. If the race gets intense enough, the pressure to cut corners goes up, and I think that's one of the strongest arguments for things like industry-wide norms and regulation — so that the "tax" is something everyone pays rather than something that just disadvantages whoever takes it most seriously.

r002.rationale: It says that taking safety seriously can differentiate Anthropic for customers and attract support from employees, indicating safety commitment can help the company attract talent.

r003.rationale: It discusses alignment, interpretability, and other safety work, but does not propose substantial upfront effort to develop measures that become inexpensive to use.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to distinguish two things. One is spending resources on safety research: hiring people, running experiments, trying to understand what your models are doing. That costs money, but it can also make your product better. Customers want models that are reliable, that follow instructions, that don’t do unexpected things. So I don’t think you should assume every dollar spent on safety is a dollar sacrificed to commercial competitiveness.

The harder case is when safety means saying, “We could release this model, and it would make us a lot of money, but we’re not confident it’s safe.” That could be a much bigger competitive disadvantage. And I don’t think there’s some clever business strategy that makes that tradeoff disappear.

Part of the hope is that you can do enough work ahead of time to make the tradeoff less painful: develop safeguards, develop ways to evaluate risks, figure out what evidence you’d need to proceed. But another part is getting the rest of the industry to face similar requirements. If a model poses a serious public risk, we shouldn’t be relying entirely on one company’s willingness to bear a cost that its competitors don’t bear.

So my answer is partly that a lot of safety work is compatible with being commercially successful, and partly that commercial incentives alone aren’t going to solve the whole problem.

r003.rationale: It proposes doing work upfront on safeguards and risk evaluation, but does not say those measures would be inexpensive to use once developed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is how much the safety work actually conflicts with making a useful product. There’s a lot of work you might call safety work—making a model more reliable, making it follow instructions, understanding when it’s going to do something unexpected—that customers also want. So I don’t think you should assume that every dollar spent on safety is a dollar that puts you further behind commercially.

Then there’s the harder case, where you really do face a tradeoff: you could release something sooner, or make it more capable, if you were willing to take more risk. I don’t think there’s a general argument that those tradeoffs will always be affordable. That’s something you have to look at as it comes up.

My hope would be that a company can stay near the frontier, do useful safety research, and help establish standards that other companies also follow. Because ultimately, if responsible behavior carries a very large competitive penalty, I wouldn’t want our whole strategy to depend on one company being willing to absorb that penalty indefinitely.
